transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Harbour Museum. My name is Louise, and I’m the events coordinator here. I’d like to tell you about our Summer Discover programme before you explore the galleries.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: This is the fifth year of the programme, and it has grown considerably. We’ve extended our opening hours on Thursdays, and entry to the permanent collection is now free. Special exhibitions still require a ticket. But the real headline this year is a series of outdoor workshops in the museum garden. We’ll be running them every Saturday throughout July and August.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: For anyone interested in family history, we have two workshops each month. These sessions are designed for young people aged thirteen to seventeen, although parents are welcome to come along. transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: One event I’d particularly recommend is the night tour. It begins at eight o’clock and lasts about ninety minutes. transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The café is open every day except Monday, when it closes for staff training. During August it will stay open until eight in the evening, so you can have dinner after a late visit.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Now, how do you book? The quickest way is through our website. The phone line is often very busy in the summer, and while you can book at reception, we only hold a limited number of places there. So I’d strongly suggest booking online before you come.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Before you explore, let me explain where everything is. You’re standing in the main entrance, marked A on your map. Directly ahead is the ticketing desk. The Lecture Theatre is at the far end of the building, past Gallery One. The Workshop Studio is beside the Lecture Theatre, with its own door onto the garden. The museum shop is by the entrance, on your right.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Now, for today’s events. At eleven o’clock, Dr Alan Pierce will give a talk on the history of the harbour. That will be in the Lecture Theatre. It’s free, but you need to collect a ticket from the desk.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The children’s craft sessions run all afternoon. They take place in the Workshop Studio, where there are large tables and plenty of materials. Parents need to stay with their children.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you’re feeling hungry, refreshments are being served in the Garden courtyard. There’s a small stall selling cakes and sandwiches, and the café is also open as usual.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The new photography exhibition, “Harbour Light”, is in Gallery Two. It features work by local photographers and runs until the end of September.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Finally, this evening’s music performance will be in Gallery One at seven o’clock. The gallery will close to other visitors at half past six so the musicians can set up. I hope you enjoy your visit.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Section 4. You will hear a lecture about bees in cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning. Today I want to talk about an animal that many people are surprised to find in cities: the bee. When we think of bees, we usually imagine wildflower meadows or orchards in the countryside. But over the past twenty years, researchers have discovered that towns and cities can be surprisingly good places for many bee species.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One reason is that cities can actually offer greater plant diversity than the farmland around them. Gardens, parks, balconies and roadside verges contain an enormous variety of flowers, often planted by people. A single city garden may contain more species than a large field of a single crop. For bees that feed on many different plants, this variety is valuable.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But flowers are only one requirement. Like all insects, bees need food, shelter and water. Water is often overlooked. Ponds, birdbaths and even shallow puddles provide the moisture that bees need, especially in hot weather.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The urban climate also affects bee behaviour. Cities are warmer than the surrounding countryside because of all the concrete and asphalt, which absorb heat. This can cause queen bees to emerge earlier in the year. In some years, queens may appear several weeks before their rural relatives. That can be an advantage if flowers are also available early, but it creates a risk if a cold spell follows.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: To study these changes, scientists need to monitor colonies closely. One technique is to place tiny microphones inside hives. The microphones record the sound of the colony, and researchers can detect changes in the bees’ buzzing that may indicate stress, disease or the loss of a queen. It’s a remarkable example of how technology can help us understand insects without opening the hive.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, not all urban habitats are equally good. A study in Melbourne, Australia, compared the bee communities in private gardens with those in public parks. The gardens supported a greater number of species. The researchers suggested that this was because gardens contained more varieties of flowers and more sheltered corners. Parks were often mown too frequently and had fewer flowering plants.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: However, small gardens on their own may not be enough to sustain a population. Connectivity matters. Roof gardens and green roofs can act as stepping stones between larger green spaces, allowing bees to move across the city. Even a small balcony can play a part if it is planted with the right flowers.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There are risks, too. One study collected pollen from urban hives and found traces of pesticides in the samples. The levels were usually low, but the finding shows that cities are not free from agricultural chemicals. Gardeners can help by avoiding pesticides and choosing native plants.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, I want to mention a citizen science project called BeeWatch. Volunteers record sightings of bees in their local area using a mobile app. The project has produced thousands of records and helped researchers identify where particular species are thriving. If you’d like to take part, the best time to record sightings is early morning, when bees are still warming up and are easier to photograph. And if you have a garden, one of the simplest things you can do is leave a pile of dead wood in a corner. Many solitary bees nest in dead wood, and it costs nothing.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, cities are not simply a poor substitute for the countryside. With thoughtful planting and a little tolerance for untidiness, they can become valuable habitats for a wide range of bees.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have some time to check your answers. This is the end of the listening test.

reading.title: The Return of the Bison
reading.subtitle: How a species brought back from the edge is reshaping the grasslands — and the argument about how to protect it

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the beginning of the nineteenth century, an estimated thirty to sixty million bison roamed the grasslands of North America. They moved in herds so large that a single herd could take days to pass. By 1884, fewer than 350 wild bison survived. Hunters, railways and government policies had turned abundance into near-extinction in less than a century. For the Plains peoples who depended on the animal for food, shelter and ceremony, the loss was cultural as well as ecological. The bison had been the centre of a way of life, and its disappearance was a deliberate part of the campaign to dismantle that life.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Bison are often described as ecosystem engineers, and the phrase is more than a compliment. Their grazing removes the tall grasses that would otherwise dominate a meadow, allowing shorter plants and wildflowers to receive light. Their wallows — shallow depressions made by rolling in the dust — collect rainwater and become temporary pools used by insects, birds and amphibians. Their hooves break up compacted soil, and their dung returns nutrients and disperses seeds. A long-term study in Kansas found that plots grazed by bison contained a greater variety of plant species than plots left ungrazed. The animals do not simply live in a landscape; they help to make it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Conservation began when the situation looked hopeless. In 1905, the American Bison Society was founded, with the aim of establishing captive herds and protected ranges. The Bronx Zoo bred animals, and in 1907 a small group was transported to the Wichita Mountains reserve in Oklahoma. These early reserves were created by government agencies and private conservation organisations, not by the tribal nations whose relationship with the bison had been broken. The programme worked, at least in the narrow sense that the species survived. By the 1930s there were several thousand bison, and the panic of extinction had given way to a new idea: that a wild animal could be managed, fenced and brought back.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Survival, however, came at a genetic cost. The modern plains bison population is descended from a remarkably small number of animals. Yellowstone’s herd, often treated as the most genetically wild, grew from roughly two dozen individuals. Early ranchers also crossed bison with cattle in an attempt to produce a hardier domestic animal. Genetic testing has since found cattle DNA in many commercial herds, although not in the Yellowstone population. Low genetic diversity leaves bison more vulnerable to disease and environmental change. Conservationists now argue about whether herds should be mixed to restore variation, or kept separate to preserve whatever distinctiveness remains.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In recent decades, the initiative has shifted. More than twenty tribal nations have signed the Buffalo Treaty, an agreement that treats the animal as a relative as well as a resource. For its signatories, restoration is not only a matter of biodiversity but of food sovereignty, education and cultural continuity. Tribal herds are also changing the scientific picture. Because they are managed by communities that rely on them, they are often monitored more closely than herds on remote public land. The treaty has helped to reconnect fragmented habitats and to place Indigenous knowledge at the centre of a conservation story from which it had been excluded.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The return of the bison has also revived an older conflict. Ranchers in the Yellowstone region worry that bison, which can carry brucellosis, may transmit the disease to cattle; the evidence for transmission in the wild is contested, but the economic consequences for a rancher would be severe. Others point to the damage bison can do to fences and crops when they leave protected areas. There is disagreement, too, about what a restored herd should be. Some argue that bison should be treated as wildlife, free to move across the landscape. Others regard them as livestock, to be owned, vaccinated and controlled. The animal has survived; the argument about its future has only become more complicated.

reading.title: Listening to the Ocean
reading.subtitle: Marine scientists are learning to read the soundscape of the sea — and discovering that noise is a form of pollution

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of human history, the sea was imagined as a place of silence. Sailors spoke of a “silent world”, and early naturalists assumed that sound could not travel far through water. That assumption was wrong. Water carries sound about four and a half times faster than air, and low-frequency sound can travel for hundreds of kilometres. The ocean is, in fact, an extraordinarily noisy place. Rain, waves, earthquakes and the clicks and calls of marine animals combine into a complex soundscape. A hydrophone lowered into the water does not record emptiness; it records a dense and constantly changing acoustic environment.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most famous example is the song of the humpback whale. Male humpbacks produce long, structured sequences of moans, cries and clicks that can last for twenty minutes and carry across an entire ocean basin. The songs are not fixed. They change gradually over months and years, and new versions spread from one population to another. Researchers have used these changes to trace migration routes and social connections. The song is also a reminder that the sea is full of information: an animal can announce its presence, attract a mate or warn a rival without ever seeing the other individual.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sound is not only communication; it is also a map. Many coral larvae are tiny, weak swimmers, yet they must find a suitable place to settle after drifting in the plankton. Experiments have shown that they are more likely to settle on surfaces near the sound of a healthy reef — the crackle of snapping shrimp, the grunts of fish — than near the relative quiet of a degraded one. The soundscape acts as a cue, allowing a larva to distinguish a living community from a dead one. Similar cues are used by some fish and crabs when choosing a habitat.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Human activity has added a new and dominant layer to this environment. Commercial shipping has increased enormously since the mid-twentieth century, and the low-frequency rumble of engines and propellers travels far through the water. In some busy shipping lanes, background noise has risen by several dozen decibels over the past seventy years. For animals that rely on low-frequency calls, the effect is like trying to hold a conversation beside a motorway. Whales may raise the volume of their calls, but this costs energy and can still fail to overcome the noise. Chronic noise has been linked to stress and to changes in feeding and migration behaviour.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If sound can damage a habitat, it can also help to repair one. In a series of experiments, researchers placed underwater speakers around patches of degraded reef and played recordings made at healthy sites. Fish arrived in greater numbers, and the patches began to accumulate the kinds of organisms that support a reef community. The technique, sometimes called acoustic enrichment, is not a substitute for reducing pollution or protecting fish stocks. But it shows that the soundscape is not merely a symptom of reef health; it can be a tool for restoring it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is turning all this listening into reliable knowledge. A single hydrophone can produce months of recordings, and the amount of acoustic data now being collected is far beyond what researchers can examine by hand. Machine learning can identify particular calls and patterns, but the models need carefully labelled examples and may fail when conditions change. Sound also tells us what is present, not why it matters. A recording can reveal that a species has returned to an area, but not whether the population is healthy. The next task for marine acoustics is therefore as much political as technical: to persuade shipping companies and governments that quieter ships and protected quiet areas are part of conservation, not an optional extra.

reading.title: The Prediction Paradox
reading.subtitle: Why experts are often poor forecasters, and what the best of them do differently

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1984, the psychologist Philip Tetlock began an experiment that would make him unpopular in certain circles. He recruited 284 experts in politics, economics and international affairs and asked them to make thousands of predictions about future events. Over the next twenty years, he collected more than 82,000 forecasts and compared them with what actually happened. The result was humbling. The experts were barely more accurate than chance, and in some cases they performed worse than a simple rule that extrapolated recent trends. The people who appeared most often on television were not the best forecasters; they were often the worst.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Tetlock borrowed a distinction from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin. Hedgehogs know one big thing: they organise the world around a single theory and interpret new events as confirmation of it. Foxes know many little things: they draw on different ideas, tolerate contradiction and are willing to revise their views. Foxes, Tetlock found, were significantly better at forecasting. The reason is not that they are more intelligent, but that they are less attached to a single story. A hedgehog who predicts that an economy will collapse may keep predicting collapse because the theory demands it; a fox notices the evidence that does not fit and adjusts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The research programme eventually became a tournament. In 2011, the Good Judgment Project invited thousands of volunteers to forecast political and economic events, with their accuracy scored against real outcomes. A small group stood out. These “superforecasters” were not necessarily experts in the regions they were predicting. What distinguished them was a set of habits. They thought in probabilities rather than certainties, broke questions into smaller parts, updated their estimates frequently and in small increments, and actively looked for evidence that might prove them wrong. They also avoided hindsight bias: after an event, they reviewed their earlier reasoning instead of simply congratulating themselves on being right.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One of the most reliable findings in the field is that crowds can beat individuals. When forecasts from many independent people are averaged, the result is usually more accurate than the typical individual forecast, and sometimes better than the best one. The effect is strengthened when forecasters are asked to explain their reasoning and when their scores are visible to others. Aggregation works because individual errors are partly random: one person overestimates a risk, another underestimates it, and the average lands closer to the truth. The lesson is not that expertise is worthless, but that no single perspective should be trusted completely.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Artificial intelligence has added a new dimension. Large language models can absorb enormous quantities of news and data and produce forecasts at a speed no human team could match. In some domains, they perform surprisingly well. Yet the evidence so far suggests that the best results come from hybrid arrangements, in which a model generates a range of possibilities and human analysts judge which are plausible, ask what the model has missed and adjust for context. The machine is good at processing; the human is good at knowing which questions matter. Neither is sufficient alone.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Forecasting also has limits that no method can remove. The most consequential events are often rare, and rare events provide little feedback from which to learn. A forecaster may be right for the wrong reasons or wrong for the right ones. When a prediction fails, it is tempting to explain the failure away; when it succeeds, it is tempting to claim credit. The result is that many people improve their confidence without improving their accuracy. Tetlock calls this “belief system defence”. The best forecasters are those who resist it, who treat their own conclusions as provisional and who keep score honestly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The practical implication is encouraging. If good forecasting were a mysterious talent, most organisations could do little to improve. But the evidence suggests that it is a discipline: a set of habits that can be taught, practised and measured. Asking better questions, assigning probabilities, seeking disconfirming evidence and reviewing outcomes are not glamorous activities. They do not produce the confident headlines that audiences reward. They do, however, produce better decisions. In a world that increasingly demands certainty, the most valuable skill may be the willingness to remain uncertain for longer.

writing.title: Task 1 — Report
writing.prompt: The bar chart below shows the percentage of adults in one country who used the internet in 2010 and 2022, by age group. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.
Write a report for a university lecturer. Do not give your opinion.
writing.modelAnswer:
The bar chart compares internet use among five age groups in a single country in 2010 and 2022. Overall, the proportion of adults using the internet rose in every age group over the twelve-year period, and the gap between younger and older users narrowed substantially.

In 2010, internet use was highest among 18–29-year-olds, at 76%, followed by the 30–44 group at 68%. Usage fell steadily with age: 45% of those aged 45–59 were online, compared with only 23% of 60–74-year-olds and just 8% of people aged 75 and over.

By 2022, the pattern had changed dramatically. Almost all 18–29-year-olds (98%) and 95% of 30–44-year-olds used the internet. The most striking increase occurred among older adults. The figure for the 45–59 group climbed to 87%, while usage among 60–74-year-olds more than tripled to 70%. Even in the oldest group, the proportion rose from 8% to 38%, although this remained well below the national average.

In short, the data show both a general expansion of internet access and a significant reduction in the age gap. Nevertheless, a clear generational difference persisted in 2022, with older adults still considerably less likely to be online than younger people.
modelHighlights: A clear overview in the introduction: overall rise plus narrowing gap.
Data is grouped logically, with 2010 and 2022 compared rather than listed mechanically.
Precise figures are used selectively, and the most striking change (older adults) is highlighted.
No opinion or speculation is included.
Vocabulary of change and comparison is varied: “climbed”, “more than tripled”, “narrowed”, “well below”.

writing.title: Task 2 — Essay
writing.prompt:
Some people believe that universities should only offer courses that lead to well-paid jobs. Others think that universities should teach subjects that benefit society, even if graduates earn less.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
instructions: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
writing.modelAnswer:
Debate about the purpose of higher education often sets economic value against social value. Some argue that universities should concentrate on courses that lead directly to well-paid employment, while others believe that subjects of wider social importance deserve support even when their graduates earn less. In my view, a healthy university system needs both, but public funding should not be determined by salary outcomes alone.

Those who favour employment-focused courses make a reasonable case. Students typically invest several years and a considerable sum in their degrees, and they are entitled to expect that their qualification will improve their job prospects. Courses in engineering, medicine, computer science and finance provide obvious routes into secure careers, and economies need these graduates. If universities expanded only in fields with little labour-market demand, they might produce disillusioned graduates with large debts and limited options. From this perspective, a degree is partly a private investment, and its economic return matters.

On the other hand, a university is not merely a training provider. Subjects such as history, philosophy, social work and the arts help societies understand themselves, preserve culture and address problems that markets do not price. A social worker or a teacher may earn less than a software engineer, but their contribution to public life is substantial. Moreover, the benefits of research in the humanities are often indirect and long-term: they shape public debate, inform policy and enrich civic life. If funding were tied only to graduate salaries, these fields would shrink, and the loss would be felt across society rather than in any single balance sheet.

In my opinion, the two aims are not as opposed as they appear. Universities should ensure that every course develops transferable skills — communication, analysis, collaboration — that graduates can use in a range of careers. At the same time, governments should support subjects of social value through grants, scholarships and public-sector pathways rather than expecting students alone to bear the risk. A law graduate may work in a commercial firm; a philosophy graduate may become a teacher, a civil servant or a technology ethicist. The value of a degree cannot be reduced to a starting salary.

In conclusion, employment outcomes are a legitimate concern, but they should not be the sole measure of a university's worth. A balanced system would prepare students for work while protecting the subjects that sustain a thoughtful and functioning society.
modelHighlights: Both views are developed fully before the writer’s own position is advanced.
The position is clear and consistent: economic and social value are both necessary, but funding should not be salary-driven.
Each paragraph has a controlling idea, explanation and example.
Cohesion is natural: “from this perspective”, “on the other hand”, “moreover”, “in conclusion”.
Precise vocabulary: “labour-market demand”, “indirect and long-term”, “transferable skills”, “public-sector pathways”.
